## Create a structured outline based on the document’s table of contents and section hierarchy  
Use the detailed Table of Contents as a roadmap to organize the information into a hierarchical structure. Map each section (e.g., Item 1 Business, Item 7 MD&A) to its subcomponents (e.g., Overview, Results of Operations) and create visual or mental branches. This helps you navigate the document efficiently, locate specific data points quickly, and build a clear mental model of how the information is organized by theme and function.

## Use color-coding or tagging to distinguish between business segments and financial disclosures  
Assign distinct colors or tags to key content types: e.g., blue for business segment descriptions (Industrial, Safety and Graphics, etc.), green for financial statements and metrics, orange for risk factors and legal disclosures, and purple for governance and executive compensation. This visual strategy leverages the document’s clear segmentation and allows you to rapidly identify and retrieve information based on category, even when reviewing large blocks of text.

## Focus on cross-referencing between the summary and detailed sections (e.g., hyperlinks in the Form 10-K summary)  
Since the document includes hyperlinked cross-references in the "Form 10-K Summary," actively follow these links as you read. For each reference (e.g., “MD&A is presented in eight sections”), locate and review the corresponding section in the detailed notes. This reinforces connections between high-level summaries and granular disclosures, improving retention by creating a network of interrelated facts.

## Develop a "segment-by-segment" comparison matrix for key products and divestitures  
Create a table or matrix that lists each business segment (Industrial, Safety and Graphics, Health Care, Electronics and Energy, Consumer) and includes columns for: major products, key markets, notable divestitures (e.g., adhesive-backed films, polymer additives), and recent acquisitions (e.g., Scott Safety). This strategy capitalizes on the document’s structured business segment reporting and helps you retain product-specific details through active comparison and categorization.

## Practice active recall by identifying specific financial disclosures tied to each segment  
For each business segment, recall and write down at least one financial metric or accounting note (e.g., revenue, goodwill, restructuring actions) referenced in the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (e.g., Note 18 for business segments, Note 5 for restructuring). This strengthens memory by linking operational content to financial reporting, which is explicitly structured in the document.
